newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: SURVEY FINDS COMPANY DIRECTORS SUPPORT REMOVAL OF TARIFFS
Most company directors believe Australia has been disadvantaged by meeting tariff reduction targets.
A survey by the Australian Institute of Company Directors and KPMG has found directors generally support the long term removal of tariffs as part of the globalisation of the Australian economy.
However, they were reluctant to see tariffs removed in the short term, because of survival concerns raised by the fragmented reform process.

While 62% of the survey's respondents indicated they believe Australia has been hurt by tariff reductions, most of the company directors still believe a global free trading environment will ultimately benefit the country.
AUSTUDY MEANS TEST TO BE REVIEWED AGAIN
The Federal Education minister has announced the Austudy means test will again face review.
This follows claims by the National Farmers' Federation that the inclusion of farm assets is making the test unfair for some country people.
Senator Amanda Vanstone says only certain aspects of the so-called Actual Means Test will be looked at.
Senator Vanstone says the February review aims to make the test of eligibility more balanced.
She says in some cases, people with company trusts and partnerships can legally minimise their taxable income giving them a much greater chance to get Austudy.
But she says other people, such as PAYE earners, can't minimise their taxable income, and therefore may miss out on the benefit.
ALLEGATIONS ELLIOTT ALLEGEDLY AUTHORISED SUSPECTEC FRAUD PAYMENTS
Federal Parliament has heard new allegations that Elders boss John Elliott authorised payments at the centre of an alleged $66 million fraud.
Labor Senator Stephen Conroy has read transcripts of previously suppressed interviews the National Crime Authority did with Mr Elliott and others involved in the foreign exchange transactions.
Mr Elliott and five others were acquitted of the charges after the judge ruled much of the evidence was inadmissible.
A Parliamentary committee, of which Senator Conroy's a member, is investigating the NCA, but chairman John Bradford refused Senator Conroy permission to raise the issue at a hearing on Monday.
Senator Conroy's attacked Mr Bradford for refusing a full and open inquiry.
He says the NCA transcripts of the interview with Mr Elliott and Mr Scanlon are very damaging because they contradict the version of events that Mr Elliott has been peddling since the trial.
He says chairman of the committee, Mr Bradford, is using his position to protect the witnesses and admitters of much.
AMBASSADOR SAYS THERE WAS NO PRESSURE FOR ARAFAT INVITATION
Israeli Ambassador to Australia, Shmuel Moyal, says his government did not pressure the Australian government over its invitation to Palestinian President Yassar Arafat, to visit Australia.
The Australian government suspended an invitation to President Arafat on Friday, which had been extended by Deputy Prime Minister, Tim Fischer, during a Middle East visit earlier this year.
Palestinian representatives described the move as undignified and unfriendly.
Ambassador Moyal says he has never discussed the invitation with either Prime Minister, John Howard or Foreign Minister, Alexander Downer.
ANTARCTICA A FUTURE GLOBAL SOURCE OF FOOD AND WATER
One of Australia's Antarctic Division's senior scientists says the world's expanding population and dwindling national resources, will see Antarctica become an important global resource.

Professor Patrick Quilty says in the next millenium the global population is set to expand to eight billion, and that could see Antarctica used as a future source of food and water. Professor Quilty says the Antarctic region cannot be quarantined from the needs of the rest of the world, especially with its capacity to produce food.
He says Australia's Antarctic program is preparing itself for the changes and pressures it will face in coming years.
AIDS COUNCIL SAYS NEEDLE EXCHANGE PROGRAMS UNDER THREAT
The head of the National Council on AIDS and Related Diseases is warning that the irresponsible behaviour of some drug users is jeopardising needle exchange programs.
Speaking at the AIDS Impact conference in Melbourne, Council chairman, Chris Puplick says needle exchange schemes have saved thousands of lives and helped reduce the incidence of HIV-Aids.
But Mr Publick says about 10% of users behave irresponsibly and jeopardise the health of the 90% of users who do return and dispose of needles properly.
His warning comes just days after Australian researchers found a plausible link between the needle exchange program and a lower incidence of HIV.
ARL QUIET ON PREFERRED NUMBER OF TEAMS FOR TOP COMPETITION
Australian Rugby League chief executive Neil Whittaker says the ARL board has not expressed a view on a preferred number of teams to play in a new elite rugby league division.
This follows the ARL's endorsement of a proposal to try and heal the rifts in the game with the setting up of new national and state competitions.
A resolution passed this morning calls on the ARL to continue negotiations with Super League.
It will also establish a sustainable number of teams in a national competition, and create state based competitions for other clubs currently at the top level.
Mr Whittaker says a negotiated result will have to be achieved because of the number of people involved who have invested a great deal of emotion and equity into the game.
